messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: knitr 0.4 is on CRAN
parts:
Hi all,

I pushed a new version of knitr to CRAN last night (Windows users need
to wait for a few more hours); news and changes can be found in:
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/NEWS

Most notable changes are:

- package option 'concordance': it is super powerful with RStudio
(currently in its daily build versions); error navigation and Rnw/pdf
sync become extremely easy (you can jump back and forth between source
and output); although Sweave invented it quite a few years ago, it has
always been a half-baked feature; now it is fully functional in
RStudio
- package option 'upload.fun': you can define your own function to
upload images to servers; for 0.3.x users, please note options
'upload' and 'imgur.key' have been removed, per suggestion of
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/173
- chunk option 'autodep': a feature borrowed from weaver package to
set up automatic dependencies among cached chunks

I'm confident to say knitr is almost a strict superset of Sweave now,
which is unexpected to me since I did not plan to implement some
features in the beginning, and I thank you all for sharing practical
experience which has greatly motivated the development. This is my
shameless summary of knitr:

Sweave + cacheSweave + pgfSweave + weaver + R2HTML::RweaveHTML +
highlight::HighlightWeaveLatex + 0.2 * brew + 0.1 * SweaveListingUtils
+ more

I think LaTeX support should be enough, and I will focus more on
HTML/markdown in the next version.

Regards,
Yihui

It seems that the dev copy of Rstudio support is limited to .Rnw
formatted documents, correct? Any idea if they plan to support the
other formats (i.e. markdown?) (Thought I'd check with you before I
bug them).

Carl

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] knitr 0.4 is on CRAN
parts:
That is what I suggested them as the next step to move too. LaTeX is
good, but it is too laborious. Simple text files like markdown
documents are way easier to start with, and I believe modern
CSS3/HTML5 techniques can replace LaTeX in many cases; when I tell
this to other people, their first question is almost always "How to
write math expressions?", and I think MathJax is pretty good. So at
least for small-scale documents, markdown can be a good choice.

Recently I discovered the book series "Learn X the hard way":
http://learncodethehardway.org/ These books are basically examples and
exercises. I'm thinking if we can start a similar book on GitHub as a
collaborative project. I feel this can grow quickly with the power of
the community.

Regards,
Yihui
